newsitem.title: USA: New Mir crewman settles in at temporary home.
newsitem.headline: New Mir crewman settles in at temporary home.

text.p: British-born astronaut Michael Foale took up residence aboard Russia's Mir space station on Saturday, relieving Jerry Linenger, who has lived and worked there since January.
The change of personnel was completed when Foale's spacesuit and other gear were safely stowed aboard the orbital outpost, about 12 hours after the shuttle's docking with Mir.
"My sleeping bag is hanging on the wall," Foale radioed mission control in Houston. "So I'd like to report that I have exchanged places with Jerry and am looking forward to my stay here."
Linenger, who had to contend with more inflight emergencies than any other astronaut since the crippled Apollo 13 moonship limped home in 1970, was to return to Earth aboard the shuttle on May 24.
"I stand relieved of duties on the Mir," he said. "It's good to be back on U.S. soil."
The 42-year-old Navy captain and doctor is looking forward to a reunion with his infant son, John, and his wife, Kathryn, who is expecting the couple's second child in June.
During Linenger's four-month tour of duty, the space station suffered a flash fire that filled it with choking smoke, breakdowns in its life support system and many other technical problems.

Mir's fortunes turned around with the arrival in April of an unmanned resupply ship carrying repair gear. With most of the ailing systems restored, NASA approved Foale's stay aboard the 11-year-old space station.

"Yes, (Mir) is in the later stages of its life, but it is not about to fall out of the sky," Frank Culbertson, who oversees NASA's shuttle-Mir programme, said. "If we thought it were unsafe, we would never have transferred Michael Foale over to it."
Atlantis docked with the sprawling Russian space complex at 10:33 p.m. EDT (0233 GMT) on Friday. It was the U.S. shuttle's sixth docking with Mir.
Less than two hours later, the hatches between the two spacecraft swung open to allow the now familiar handshake between a U.S. shuttle commander and his Russian counterpart.

The shuttle astronauts offered Mir's Russian crew, Vasily Tsibliev and Alexander Lazutkin, a traditional Russian welcoming gift of bread and salt and brought Linenger the pretzels he had craved during his time in space.
"That was a perfect-looking docking," mission control's Chris Hadfield told the shuttle crew soon after the docking ports of the two spacecraft slipped together 245 miles (390 km) above the Adriatic.
"It's great to back here on Mir. It's a beautiful sight out the window," said Atlantis commander Charles Precourt, who flew on the first shuttle mission to Mir in 1995.
The shuttle arrived at Mir carrying a record 4,000 pounds (1,800 kg) of supplies and equipment, including repair gear to patch up a leaky cooling system.
One of the first items to be manhandled across to Mir was a bulky oxygen generator, about the size of an electric water heater.

The so-called Elektron device was a last-minute addition to Atlantis' cargo. The Russian space authorities rushed it to the shuttle's launch site after problems with Mir's life support systems. It uses electricity to generate breathing oxygen from waste water and will provide a crucial backup to a malfunctioning older system.

Foale is the fifth NASA astronaut to live on Mir. He will be followed by two more U.S. astronauts. The U.S. space agency plans to start building a new space station with Russia and other international partners in June 1998.
